Subject: What we got wrong about collisions on Wellsford Road

By Nell Garside

On 2 November, the Western Ledger published an analysis saying that Wellsford Road had the highest number of injury collisions of any road in Bristol: 41 between 2021 and 2025. That was wrong.

The correct figure is 23, placing Wellsford Road sixth in the city, not first. We corrected the table and added a note to the article on 6 November, but a line at the bottom of the page is not enough to explain a mistake of this size.

The original article has had more than 48,000 views. We know the wrong number travelled, and that residents have been left to deal with the concern it caused. Parents have asked whether it is safe to walk their children to Wellsford Primary. I am sorry that our reporting added to that worry.

The Fishponds Streets Forum challenged the figure after one of its members went back through the published Department for Transport data and could not get close to 41. She was right. We should have caught the error before publication, and we are grateful to the forum for asking us to look again.

The mistake happened when we joined the collision records to the roads on which they occurred. That process duplicated some collision-and-road pairs, so the same collision was counted twice on the same road. When we removed the duplicate entries, 18 came out of the Wellsford Road total. We now count each collision only once for each road on which it appears.

We reran the whole citywide table. Kingsmere Road’s total changed from 34 to 32, Alder Hill remained at 31, Tanner’s Way changed from 29 to 28, and Crossfield Road from 27 to 26. Hambrook Lane is now fifth, with 24, followed by Wellsford Road with 23. No other road moved more than two places.

The responsibility for the error is ours as a desk. Readers should be able to rely on our checks, and in this case those checks were not good enough.

The corrected figure does not mean there is nothing to worry about on Wellsford Road. Twenty-three injury collisions are still 23 collisions in which people were hurt; three were serious. These figures alone cannot tell a parent whether a particular walk to school is safe, and I do not want the correction to be read as a claim that the road is fine.

From now on, we will publish the cleaned data and code alongside our ranked tables, so readers can see how we reached the figures. A second analyst will also reproduce each ranked table before it is published.

The forum has invited us to its open meeting at Fishponds Library on 17 November at 7pm. I would like to come and answer residents’ questions in person.
